title: AI Scientists Discover De Novo Antimicrobial Peptides with 3.5× Greater Predicted Potency
author: EurekaLabs
excerpt: Our AI Scientist Team achieves results that match or improve the best performance for eight of the ten peptide templates of a leading antimicrobial peptide model. It generates de novo drug candidates at only 17–36% sequence similarity to anything in nature, with 3.5× higher predicted potency.
content:
*Demonstrating how an AI Scientist Team can move beyond optimizing known molecules to discovering entirely new drug candidates while satisfying multiple biological objectives.*

**If you read one thing:** Our [AI Scientist Team](/posts/multi-agent-ai-scientist-protein-design) achieves results that match or improve the best performance for eight of the ten peptide templates of a leading antimicrobial peptide model. It generates de novo drug candidates at only 17–36% sequence similarity to anything in nature, with 3.5× higher predicted potency.

Antimicrobial resistance is one of the most pressing challenges in modern medicine. Particularly concerning are multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens such as *Acinetobacter baumannii*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae* and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. Their protective outer membranes make them exceptionally difficult to treat with conventional antibiotics.

Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative. Rather than targeting a single bacterial protein, they can kill bacteria by disrupting their membranes. However, designing effective therapeutic peptides is challenging: increasing antimicrobial potency can also increase toxicity against beneficial bacteria, while the enormous sequence space makes experimental exploration prohibitively expensive.

This is precisely the kind of challenge our AI Scientist Team is designed to address.

We evaluated our system against ApexGO (Torres, Zeng, Wan, Maus, Gardner and de la Fuente-Nunez, *Nature Machine Intelligence*, May 2026), a recently published approach to computational antimicrobial peptide optimization. Our results demonstrate three important capabilities:

- **Benchmark competitiveness:** Our system matches or improves upon published ApexGO results under the same benchmark conditions.
- **De novo molecular discovery:** It identifies entirely new peptide sequences with only 17–36% similarity to natural templates and 3.5× greater predicted potency than benchmark-constrained designs.
- **Multi-objective optimization:** It simultaneously optimizes antimicrobial potency and selectivity, satisfying biological constraints throughout the discovery process.

Together, these results demonstrate the potential of our AI Scientist Team to move beyond incremental molecular optimization toward genuinely novel drug discovery.

## Benchmarking against ApexGO

ApexGO is an impressive recent approach to antimicrobial peptide optimization. It combines a transformer variational autoencoder with Bayesian optimization to improve peptide sequences while maintaining at least 75% sequence similarity to their natural templates.

The experimental results are compelling: the authors synthesized 100 optimized compounds, reporting an 85% experimental hit rate and a 72% success rate in improving activity against Gram-negative pathogens. Several compounds also demonstrated promising results in preclinical mouse models of *A. baumannii* infection.

This provides a meaningful benchmark against which to evaluate our system.

We therefore started with the same optimization problem: the same APEX 1.1 prediction oracle, the same eleven-strain panel, the same antimicrobial objective and the same 75% sequence-similarity constraint.

Every MIC in this post is a prediction from that oracle rather than a wet-lab measurement, as is every number we are compared against, because the published baseline is scored by the same instrument. Both sides are therefore measured with the same ruler, which is what makes the comparison a fair one. Experimental validation of the new candidates is the next step, and it is already under way.

![Ten peptide templates: our design against the published ApexGO optimum for each, scored by the same oracle](/blog/figures/fig106_designs_against_the_published_optima_anon.png)

*Figure 1. One row per peptide template, under the benchmark's own rules. The open ring is the published ApexGO optimum, the filled diamond our system's design, and the connecting line the difference between them. Lower MIC means greater potency.*

Our system improves on the published optimum for four of the ten templates and reproduces it exactly on four more: those four agree to within 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁵ µmol/l, which is five to seven orders of magnitude inside the oracle's reproducibility of 0.01 µmol/l, the tolerance, measured across devices and batch sizes, within which the same peptide scores the same twice. On the two remaining templates our design finishes marginally behind, by 0.89 and 0.01 µmol/l.

Across the ten templates, the mean MIC against the seven Gram-negative strains decreases from **36.39 to 33.90 µmol/l**, a 6.8% mean improvement. Lower MIC indicates greater antimicrobial potency.

A few percent is the honest size of the gain here, and that is the point of this section rather than a caveat to it: the benchmark is a narrow, heavily worked problem whose published solutions were synthesized and tested in the laboratory, and we match or beat them on eight of ten templates under conditions none of which we chose. That establishes the system as a legitimate optimizer. The large gains appear once the benchmark's own constraint is lifted.

**Our system demonstrates competitive performance against an established approach, providing a foundation for exploring a much larger molecular space.**

## Beyond optimization: discovering entirely new drug candidates

Most existing computational peptide-design approaches focus on generating or optimizing sequences that resemble known antimicrobial peptides. Discovering entirely new candidates, far removed from natural templates, presents a considerably harder challenge.

This is where our AI Scientist Team demonstrates a particularly interesting capability: it can explore molecular sequence space beyond the neighborhood of known molecules while maintaining the biological requirements of the discovery problem.

To investigate this capability, we removed the 75% sequence-similarity restriction and changed nothing else: the same prediction oracle, the same strain panel, the same antimicrobial objective.

**The selectivity requirement stayed in force.** Every de novo design reported below was held to the same biological rule as the benchmark-constrained ones, a predicted MIC above 32 µmol/l against all four Gram-positive strains, and the requirement sits inside the objective our system designs against rather than being applied afterwards as a filter.

![Predicted potency plotted against sequence similarity to the nearest natural template, for natural templates, benchmark-constrained designs and de novo designs](/blog/figures/fig107_potency_against_novelty_anon3.png)

*Figure 2. Each point is one peptide. Further left means further from any natural sequence; lower means more potent. The shaded band on the right is the region the benchmark's 75% similarity constraint confines a design to. The three populations separate cleanly, and the de novo designs occupy the lower-left corner, novel and potent at once.*

The results reveal a striking separation between three populations. Natural templates sit at the top right of the plot, with 100% sequence similarity to themselves and a median MIC of 352 µmol/l. Benchmark-constrained designs improve substantially, reaching a median MIC of 34.2 µmol/l, but remain within the predefined similarity boundary. De novo designs occupy a very different region: despite having only **17–36% sequence similarity** to their nearest natural templates, they achieve a median MIC of just **9.7 µmol/l**.

This represents a **3.5× improvement in predicted potency** over benchmark-constrained designs, achieved with the selectivity requirement applied throughout. Not one of these designs buys its potency by giving up selectivity: every one holds all four Gram-positive strains above the 32 µmol/l threshold.

The gain is uniform rather than selective: every one of the ten template families improves, by between **18× and 46×** over its natural starting sequence. No single exceptional candidate carries the result. Natural antimicrobial peptides are unoptimized starting material, so this figure measures the distance traveled from nature; the measure of final quality is the 3.5× against designs that were themselves optimized.

The most potent candidate is particularly interesting: a **12-amino-acid peptide with a predicted MIC of 3.85 µmol/l that also meets the selectivity requirement against all four Gram-positive strains**. Its worst-case predicted Gram-positive MIC is 59.7 µmol/l, comfortably above the required 32 µmol/l threshold.

This is more than an incremental improvement to a known molecule. It demonstrates the ability of our system to identify entirely new molecular candidates with substantially improved predicted properties while respecting multiple biological requirements.

## Potency without sacrificing selectivity

Antimicrobial potency alone is not sufficient for a viable therapeutic candidate.

A highly cationic and hydrophobic peptide might disrupt bacterial membranes effectively, but it could also damage beneficial bacteria. In therapeutic development, selectivity is therefore just as important as potency.

We explicitly incorporated this requirement into the optimization problem: candidates must maintain a MIC above 32 µmol/l against all four Gram-positive strains while maximizing activity against the seven Gram-negative pathogens.

![Mean Gram-negative MIC plotted against the lowest Gram-positive MIC for every design, with the 32 micromolar selectivity threshold marked](/blog/figures/fig108_potency_and_selectivity_anon.png)

*Figure 3. Potency on one axis, selectivity on the other. The 32 µmol/l line is the selectivity requirement: every design must lie on the permitted side of it against all four Gram-positive strains. Every design reported here does.*

The figure illustrates the relationship between antimicrobial potency and selectivity. The 32 µmol/l threshold separates candidates satisfying the selectivity requirement from those that do not.

**Every reported design satisfies the selectivity constraint**, including the most potent of them.

The most potent candidate achieves a predicted Gram-negative MIC of 3.85 µmol/l while maintaining a worst-case Gram-positive MIC of 59.7 µmol/l, nearly twice the required threshold.

Releasing the similarity constraint does move the set slightly closer to the selectivity wall: the de novo designs' median worst-case Gram-positive MIC is 32.6 µmol/l, against 34.2 µmol/l for the benchmark-constrained set. Every design in both sets is feasible, none incurs any constraint penalty, because the objective requires selectivity; the next iteration rewards headroom above the threshold rather than merely requiring it.

The important result is that our system does not simply pursue peptides with maximum antimicrobial activity. It identifies candidates that balance antimicrobial potency and selectivity simultaneously.

## From generative models to constraint-aware molecular discovery

Most computational peptide-design approaches rely on generative models that learn from known antimicrobial peptides and propose new sequences. However, generating plausible molecules is not the same as discovering molecules that satisfy multiple interacting biological requirements.

A common strategy is to generate candidates first and subsequently filter or re-rank them according to additional objectives and constraints. This can be highly inefficient: in ApexGO's published benchmark comparisons, only 22.2%, 10.8% and 0.2% of HydrAMP proposals satisfied the 75% sequence-similarity constraint at three decoder temperatures. PepDiffusion generated 10,000 sequences, none of which met the constraint.

**Our approach is fundamentally different. We use an AI Scientist Team as an integrated molecular discovery system, rather than relying on a standalone generative model.**

The system incorporates objectives and feasibility constraints directly into the iterative optimization process. Antimicrobial potency across seven Gram-negative strains, selectivity against four Gram-positive strains and the relevant feasibility requirements are evaluated together throughout the design process.

This allows the AI Scientist Team to direct its exploration toward candidates that satisfy the actual requirements of the discovery problem, rather than generating large numbers of molecules that must subsequently be discarded.

The underlying architecture and the roles of the individual AI scientists are described in our companion post: [A Multi-Agent AI Scientist Team for Protein Optimization](/posts/multi-agent-ai-scientist-protein-design).

Crucially, the same approach can incorporate additional properties such as solubility, cytotoxicity, stability, manufacturability and resistance risk. These become further optimization objectives or constraints within the discovery process, rather than independent filters applied after candidate generation.

## Toward a new paradigm in molecular discovery

Antimicrobial peptide discovery provides a particularly useful demonstration of our approach because it combines an enormous molecular space with competing biological objectives and explicit feasibility requirements.

But the underlying challenge is much broader.

In drug discovery, a promising molecule must rarely optimize just one property. Potency, selectivity, stability, solubility, toxicity and manufacturability all influence whether a candidate can progress toward a viable therapeutic. These requirements interact, and improving one property can easily compromise another.

The three capabilities shown here address exactly that difficulty, and they build on one another: the AI Scientist Team is competitive with an established approach under identical benchmark conditions, it remains competitive once the similarity constraint that defined the benchmark is removed and the designs move far away from known templates, and it does both while holding a selectivity requirement throughout rather than imposing it afterwards. Benchmark competitiveness alone would show only that the system is a credible optimizer; de novo discovery alone would be unconvincing without the constraint; it is the combination that matters for a therapeutic program.

Rather than simply generating molecules or optimizing individual properties, we are building AI systems that actively explore molecular space, reason about competing objectives and systematically discover candidates that satisfy the requirements of real-world applications.

The antimicrobial peptide results provide an initial demonstration of this capability. The next step is to take the most promising candidates into experimental validation and establish how well the computational improvements translate into biological activity.

---

### Key results

| Capability | Result |
|---|---|
| Benchmark performance | Improves on 4 of 10 ApexGO optima; reproduces 4 exactly |
| Benchmark potency | Mean MIC: 36.39 → 33.90 µmol/l (6.8%) |
| De novo discovery | 17–36% similarity to nearest natural templates |
| Potency improvement | 3.5× over benchmark-constrained designs |
| Consistency | All 10 template families improve |
| Best predicted candidate | 3.85 µmol/l |
| Selectivity | Required throughout, including de novo: all candidates satisfy the 32 µmol/l threshold |
| Best candidate's Gram-positive MIC | 59.7 µmol/l |

**The broader implication:** We are moving from AI that modifies existing molecules toward AI Scientist Teams that discover entirely new candidates while optimizing multiple biological objectives simultaneously.

That is the foundation of a scalable AI-driven molecular discovery platform.

---

### Work with us on the next campaign

We run these campaigns against our partners' targets: a defined objective, an explicit set of constraints, and a ranked shortlist of candidates to take into the laboratory. If you are developing peptide or protein therapeutics and want the next shortlist to come from a system that optimizes every requirement at once, we would like to hear from you.

---

*Technical note: All MIC values reported in this analysis are predictions from the APEX 1.1 ensemble oracle, the same benchmark prediction instrument used to evaluate the published baselines. They are computational estimates, not experimentally measured MIC values. The figures are generated directly from the stored oracle records. Experimental validation of the newly identified candidates remains an important next step.*

title: Building a Multi-Agent AI Scientist Team for Protein Drug Development
author: Dr. Claus Horn
excerpt: How we are building an AI Scientist Team as a multi-agent research organization for protein drug development, and how we validate it by replaying real laboratory campaigns.
content:
Computational protein design has a measurement problem: models produce confident predictions, but those predictions are only imperfectly related to whether a molecule actually works in the lab. Public protein-design competitions make this gap visible. Published standardized wet-lab results show hit rates across campaigns ranging from 2.5% to 14%. The central challenge is therefore not simply to generate promising molecules, but to decide which ones deserve an experimental slot, and to learn from the results.

## A Multi-Agent Research Organization

We are building an AI Scientist Team as a research organization with specialized responsibilities, rather than a single general-purpose agent. A single agent tasked with running an entire campaign must generate ideas, evaluate its own proposals, allocate resources and judge its own confidence. Separating these responsibilities creates independent perspectives and makes it easier to challenge weak assumptions.

![Multi-Agent Research Organization](/blog/figures/researchOrganization.png)

The organization consists of several specialized roles:

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Spec Reader** | Converts the campaign brief into explicit objectives, positive and negative targets, constraints and evaluation criteria. |
| **Target Biologist** | Prepares target structures, identifies relevant epitopes and defines the molecular interactions to promote or avoid. |
| **Principal Investigator** | Coordinates the campaign, allocates computational and experimental resources, and sets decision and stopping criteria. |
| **Generators** | Explore parallel design strategies, including diffusion-based design, sequence optimization, nanobody and antibody design, and grafting. |
| **Oracle** | Evaluates candidates using co-folding, structural analysis and energetic calculations. |
| **Specificity Counter-screen** | Tests whether candidates interact with unintended targets or molecular configurations. |
| **Developability Specialist** | Assesses expression risks, aggregation, free cysteines, format constraints and other developability criteria. |
| **Critic** | Challenges assumptions, identifies metric gaming, checks for data leakage and scrutinises confidence estimates. |
| **Biosecurity Gate** | Performs sequence screening and dual-use review before designs leave the system. |

Each role produces structured outputs that the next stage can inspect and use. The workflow is therefore not just a sequence of conversations: it is an auditable process in which decisions, evidence and computational results are explicitly connected.



### Specialized Intelligence for Different Chemical Contexts

General-purpose foundation models are trained to perform across broad distributions of tasks. This makes them powerful starting points, but their reliability can vary substantially across molecular configurations, chemical environments and interaction types.

Our approach adds specialized, task-specific focus modules. Rather than treating every model prediction as equally reliable, these modules learn when to trust, discount or combine the outputs of underlying models for a particular chemical context.

The modules integrate several complementary sources of evidence:

- **Pretrained molecular embeddings**, capturing information from protein and molecular language models.
- **Structural features**, extracted from structure prediction and protein–protein co-folding.
- **Dynamic features**, derived from molecular-dynamics simulations, including conformational flexibility, stability and interaction persistence.

These information channels and evaluation components can be activated or deactivated individually during optimization. The system can therefore learn not only how to interpret a given source of evidence, but also when that source is useful for a particular subtask. We fine-tune focus modules for individual chemical tasks rather than relying exclusively on one global model to handle every situation.

The distinction is important: the research agents coordinate the scientific workflow; the focus modules provide specialized, learned interpretation of molecular evidence.

![Campaign Loop](/blog/figures/campaign_loop.png)



## Validation: Replaying Real Laboratory Campaigns

Evaluating an autonomous design system is hard because the ground truth lives in a wet lab, and a model that merely agrees with another model proves nothing. We therefore evaluate ours against measurements that already exist.

Public design competitions have released many thousand protein and peptide designs together with the binding affinities measured for them, successes and failures alike, across more than twenty targets. We hold these measurements out and replay each campaign as a closed loop. In each round the system proposes a batch of candidates; we reveal only the real laboratory result for that batch, exactly as a lab would return it; the system updates and proposes again. It never sees a measurement it has not “paid” for with an experiment.

The question this answers is not *can the system recognize a good binder*, but *how few experiments does it need to find one*. What we observe (see figure below), performance climbs steeply over the first rounds as the system learns what distinguishes the binders of this particular target from the near-misses, then saturates once the informative molecules in the pool have been exhausted, the point at which further experiments stop buying information. We report the round at which that happens, the hit rate at saturation against a no-learning control drawn from the same pool, and the best affinity recovered against the best affinity the pool contains.

Across held-out targets, the system reaches the quality of the published human campaigns in roughly a quarter of the experiments those campaigns required. We weight most heavily the datasets released after our models were trained, and we report those separately.

![Evaluation Loop](/blog/figures/retrospective-loop-figure.svg)

*Retrospective evaluation establishes efficiency: the system is choosing from molecules that already exist.*

## Learning Across Campaigns

A system that starts from scratch with every new target loses much of the knowledge accumulated in previous experiments. We want the opposite: a research organization that becomes more capable with every campaign.

Three forms of knowledge persist:

**Calibration from experimental outcomes.** Public campaign data allow us to estimate how reliably different models and design methods perform in different contexts. Instead of asking only what a model predicts, we ask how often predictions of that kind have corresponded to successful experimental outcomes. These calibration models can then inform subsequent design and selection decisions.

**Failure memory.** Every candidate is stored with its provenance: the generator, binding mode, target context, evaluation results and reasons for rejection. When a new target resembles an earlier one, relevant successes and failures can inform the next campaign. This prevents the system from repeatedly exploring attractive approaches that have already failed.

**Evolving scientific heuristics.** Design rules, evaluation criteria and resource-allocation strategies are versioned and revised as new evidence emerges. They become persistent, inspectable components of the system rather than instructions that researchers must manually reconstruct for each project.

The objective is a compounding research capability: later campaigns should benefit measurably from the evidence and experience accumulated in earlier ones.

## A System That Can Run Campaigns

The agent organization depends on a reliable computational foundation. Beneath the reasoning layer is a collection of structured tools for structure prediction and co-folding, diffusion-based design, sequence optimization, antibody and nanobody design, energetic evaluation, molecular dynamics and developability analysis.

Each tool has defined inputs and outputs. Agents can request computations and interpret their results, but quantitative measurements come from the tools themselves. This separation makes decisions reproducible.

The infrastructure also needs to support campaigns at scale. Candidates pass through progressively more expensive evaluation stages: inexpensive filters screen large sets, while more demanding structural and physical calculations are reserved for promising candidates. Parallel execution allows independent design strategies to run simultaneously, and a provenance record preserves the complete history of every candidate.

**Discovery as a portfolio optimization problem**

A protein-design campaign has a finite experimental budget. The objective is not simply to select the twenty highest-scoring sequences. It is to maximise the probability of experimental success under uncertainty.

Candidates generated by the same method, scaffold or binding hypothesis can be highly correlated. Selecting only the top-ranked designs may therefore create a portfolio of near-duplicates: if the underlying assumption is wrong, they can all fail together.

A better strategy distributes experimental resources across genuinely different hypotheses, weighs candidates according to calibrated confidence, and considers the information that each experiment could provide. A failed experiment should still improve the next decision.

This is why we build an organization that can generate, challenge, evaluate and learn, not merely a model that ranks sequences. Ultimately, the value of an AI Scientist Team will be measured not by the sophistication of its architecture, but by the quality of the molecules it helps discover and the experimental resources it saves along the way.

**Safety is at the heart of what we do**

Safety is integrated into this workflow. Sequence screening and dual-use review operate as explicit gates, with recorded outcomes, rather than relying on an agent's judgement or a final manual check. The same provenance infrastructure that supports scientific learning makes designs traceable and decisions auditable.

title: From Text to Molecules: Choosing a Problem That Can Tell Us We Are Wrong
author: EurekaLabs
excerpt: Our first multi-agent systems wrote grant proposals and literature reviews. They worked, and we could not prove it: a document has no fast ground truth. A designed molecule does, which is why the AI Scientist Team now designs molecules.
content:
**If you read one thing:** We kept the architecture and changed the object. Our [AI Scientist Team](/posts/multi-agent-ai-scientist-protein-design) was built to do scientific work that a machine can be graded on, and the grade has to come from outside the machine. A document cannot supply one in any useful time. A designed molecule can, in weeks, from an instrument that has no opinion about us.

## What the first systems taught us

In 2025 we built two multi-agent systems for the research workflow: an assistant that takes a research idea to a submission-ready NIH proposal, and one that turns a project description into a literature review with the citations retrieved rather than recalled. Both are real systems, both ran, and the engineering in them is the engineering we still use: agents with separate responsibilities, retrieval instead of recollection, an independent critic that scores the work against a rubric it did not write, and a record of why every decision was made.

What we could not do was tell how good they were.

A grant proposal is graded by a panel, months later, on a scale that mixes the quality of the writing with the reputation of the applicant, the fit to that year's priorities and the size of the pool. A literature review is graded by a reviewer who will not say which of your sentences changed their mind. In both cases the signal arrives late, arrives once, and arrives mixed with everything else about the project. You can run such a system for a year and learn almost nothing about whether its tenth campaign was better than its first.

For a product, that is survivable. For a research organization intended to improve with use, it is fatal. A system that cannot be told it was wrong cannot get better in any direction you can defend.

## What a molecule gives you that a document does not

A designed protein is a claim with a date on it. You write a sequence, you have it made, and within weeks an assay returns a number: it binds or it does not, it kills the organism or it does not, it is selective or it is toxic. Nobody on our side chooses that number. It is not an opinion about our method and it does not care how sophisticated the system that produced the candidate was.

That property is what makes design the right first problem for an AI Scientist Team, and it has three consequences we build on directly.

**It makes every campaign a measurement of the system, not only of the molecule.** We can ask how many experiments the system needed to reach a given quality, and compare that to how many a published human campaign needed for the same target. That is a number about the engine.

**It makes failure informative.** A rejected proposal teaches you very little. A candidate that was predicted to bind and did not is a located error: a generator, a binding hypothesis and a scoring context that can be stored, recognized when it recurs, and stopped from being proposed again.

**It makes the work an asset rather than a saving.** A literature review that takes two days instead of two weeks is a time saving, and a time saving is worth what the time costs. A molecule that works is property.

## What stayed the same

The pivot is narrower than it sounds. The research organization is the same idea it was: a set of specialized roles, a principal investigator allocating a finite experimental budget, generators proposing in parallel, a critic whose job is to attack the team's own conclusions, a gate that candidates pass before anything leaves the system. What changed is the oracle. In the proposal assistant, the critic scored against the NIH's published criteria. In a design campaign, the final critic is an instrument in a laboratory, and the intermediate critics are structural and energetic calculations whose agreement with that instrument we can measure and keep measuring.

Everything else follows from that substitution. Because the grader is external, we can run the same engine against problems that have nothing to do with each other and compare the results: antibiotic peptides, inhibitors for neurodegenerative disease, binders judged in a blind externally scored competition, enzymes that are not therapeutics at all. Each campaign is chosen to prove something the others cannot, and each is graded by somebody who is not us.

## The engine, not the campaign

The useful unit here is not any single result. It is the loop: propose, spend an experiment, learn, propose again, and carry what was learned into the next target. Calibration of how far each model can be trusted in each chemical context, a memory of what has already failed, design rules that are versioned rather than remembered. A campaign that benefits from the nine before it is a different asset from nine campaigns run in parallel by the same tool.

That is the thing we are building, and it is the reason the work moved from text to molecules. We needed a problem that answers back.

### Work with us on the next campaign

We run campaigns with partners who have a target and an assay. If you have one, we would like to hear what it is.

title: Multi-Agent Assistants for Grant Proposals and Literature Reviews
author: EurekaLabs Engineering
excerpt: Two early multi-agent systems from 2025: nine agents taking a research idea to a submission-ready NIH proposal, and six turning a project description into a related work section. Both put an independent reviewer between the work and the claim.
content:
*Building sophisticated multi-agent systems for scientific research*

> **A note added in November 2026.** This post describes work from the summer of 2025, when our multi-agent systems were pointed at the research workflow rather than at molecules. It is left here as it was written. The architecture it describes, specialized agents with separate responsibilities and an independent critic scoring the work against a rubric it did not write, is the architecture we now run over protein design campaigns, where the rubric is a laboratory measurement rather than a review panel. We explain the move in [From text to molecules](/posts/from-text-to-molecules).

We built two systems that summer, on the same architecture and with the same conviction: that the way to make a language model do serious scholarly work is to stop asking one model to do all of it. The first takes a research idea to a submission-ready grant proposal. The second takes a project description to a related work section. Both are described below.

# Part One: The Grant Proposal Assistant

## The Challenge

Every year, researchers spend countless months crafting grant proposals—time that could be better spent on actual discovery. The process is notoriously complex: navigating intricate NIH requirements, synthesizing vast amounts of literature, ensuring compliance with ever-changing regulations, and presenting compelling scientific narratives. Even brilliant researchers often struggle with proposal writing, not because they lack scientific merit, but because grant writing is a specialized skill distinct from research expertise.

What if we could change that? What if AI could handle the heavy lifting of proposal development, allowing researchers to focus on what they do best—advancing human knowledge?

## Our Solution: A Multi-Agent AI Research Assistant

We set out to build something unprecedented: an AI system specifically designed to guide researchers from initial idea to submission-ready grant proposal. But this wasn't going to be a simple chatbot. The complexity of research proposal development demanded a more sophisticated approach.

Our solution employs **nine specialized AI agents** working in concert, each focusing on a different aspect of proposal development. Think of it as assembling a dream team of experts—a literature specialist, a compliance officer, a scientific critic, a writing coach—all powered by advanced AI and coordinated through intelligent orchestration.

### The Nine-Agent Architecture

Here's how our system works:

```
Researcher's Idea
       ↓
[Intent Detector] ——→ Identifies optimal funding programs
       ↓
[Literature Retriever] ——→ Searches scientific databases
       ↓
[Draft Generator] ——→ Creates initial content
       ↓
[Citation Suggester] ——→ Finds supporting evidence
       ↓
[Research Critic] ——→ Evaluates using NIH criteria
       ↓
[Compliance Checker] ——→ Ensures format adherence
       ↓
[Red Team Evaluator] ——→ Assesses risks and ethics
       ↓
[Content Rewriter] ——→ Polishes for clarity and impact
       ↓
[Document Exporter] ——→ Generates final proposal
```

Each agent is a specialist. The **Intent Detector** analyzes a researcher's goals and determines whether they should apply for an R01, R21, or another program type. The **Literature Retriever** automatically searches PubMed and Crossref, finding relevant papers and assessing their relevance. The **Research Critic** applies the same 1-9 scoring rubric that actual NIH study sections use, providing researchers with realistic assessments before submission.

## Technical Achievements

### Real-Time Multi-Agent Orchestration

The technical heart of our system is a LangGraph-based orchestration engine that manages complex interactions between agents. Unlike simple AI chatbots that process requests linearly, our system maintains sophisticated state across multiple agents, allowing for iterative refinement and collaborative intelligence.

**Measurable Achievement**: Our system can simultaneously coordinate up to 9 different AI agents, each running specialized prompts optimized for their domain, while maintaining conversation context and project state across sessions.

### Adaptive Requirements Engine

One of our breakthrough innovations is a modular requirements system that can adapt to any funding agency. Instead of hard-coding NIH rules, we built a dynamic engine that ingests requirement specifications and automatically configures compliance checking, section templates, and evaluation criteria.

**Measurable Achievement**: The system currently supports NIH R01/R21 and NSF general requirements out of the box, with the ability to add new funding bodies through JSON configuration files—no code changes required.

### Automatic Critique Integration

Perhaps most importantly, our system provides continuous feedback. Every time a researcher edits a section, the Research Critic agent automatically evaluates the content using official NIH review criteria, providing scores and specific suggestions for improvement.

**Measurable Achievement**: The critique system processes content in under 30 seconds and provides structured feedback including numerical scores (1-9 NIH scale), specific strengths and weaknesses, and actionable improvement recommendations.

### Intelligent Literature Integration

Our Literature Retriever doesn't just find papers—it understands context. It searches across multiple academic databases, assesses relevance to the specific research proposal, and suggests how each citation might be used to strengthen different sections of the proposal.

**Measurable Achievement**: The system can search and analyze up to 50 relevant papers in under 2 minutes, providing relevance scores and specific recommendations for how each citation supports the research narrative.

## User Experience Innovation

### Conversational Research Development

We transformed the traditionally document-centric proposal writing process into a natural conversation. Researchers can simply describe their research ideas in plain language, and the system guides them through the entire development process.

The interface seamlessly blends chat-based interaction with rich document editing. Researchers can ask questions like "How can I strengthen my methodology section?" or "What are the current NIH salary cap limits?" and receive immediate, contextual assistance.

### Real-Time Compliance Monitoring

Gone are the days of discovering formatting violations at the last minute. Our system continuously monitors compliance with funding agency requirements, providing real-time feedback on page limits, budget constraints, and required sections.

**Visual indicators** show completion status for each section, compliance scores update automatically, and the system generates comprehensive checklists ensuring nothing is missed.

### Collaborative Intelligence

The system learns from each interaction, building a knowledge base of successful proposal patterns and reviewer preferences. This creates a virtuous cycle where the AI becomes more helpful over time.

## Technical Architecture Highlights

### Modular AI Integration

We built our system with flexibility in mind. While currently powered by Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4, the architecture supports multiple AI providers, ensuring resilience and enabling us to leverage the best models for different tasks.

### Scalable State Management

Managing complex, multi-step workflows across AI agents required sophisticated state management. Our LangGraph implementation maintains conversation context, project history, and agent coordination seamlessly.

### Performance Optimization

Despite coordinating multiple AI agents, our system maintains responsive performance through intelligent caching, parallel processing, and optimized prompt engineering.

**Measurable Achievement**: End-to-end proposal section generation (from user input to polished draft with citations and critique) completes in under 2 minutes.

## Real-World Impact Potential

### Democratizing Grant Writing

Our system levels the playing field, giving early-career researchers and those at under-resourced institutions access to the same level of proposal development support traditionally available only through expensive consultants or well-connected mentors.

### Accelerating Scientific Discovery

By reducing proposal development time from months to weeks, we free up researchers to spend more time on actual research. The system's ability to identify optimal funding opportunities also helps ensure good research finds appropriate support.

### Improving Success Rates

Through continuous compliance monitoring and expert-level critique, the system helps researchers avoid common pitfalls that lead to rejection, potentially improving overall funding success rates across the scientific community.

## Looking Forward

This project represents more than just an AI application—it's a glimpse into the future of scientific research support. We've demonstrated that sophisticated multi-agent AI systems can tackle complex, domain-specific challenges that require both technical precision and creative insight.

The implications extend beyond grant writing. The same architectural principles—specialized agents, intelligent orchestration, domain-specific knowledge integration—could transform other aspects of research workflow: literature review, experimental design, peer review, and scientific writing.

### What Makes This Different

While there are many AI writing tools, ours is purpose-built for the unique challenges of scientific proposal development. It understands NIH review criteria, knows the difference between R01 and R21 requirements, and can navigate the complex landscape of federal research funding.

More importantly, it's designed by researchers, for researchers. Every feature addresses real pain points we've experienced firsthand in the research community.

## The Technology Behind the Magic

Our system represents several key innovations in AI application development:

1. **Domain-Specific Multi-Agent Architecture**: Unlike general-purpose AI assistants, our agents are trained specifically for research proposal development, with deep knowledge of funding agencies, review processes, and scientific writing conventions.

2. **Dynamic Requirements Adaptation**: The ability to quickly adapt to new funding opportunities and agencies through modular configuration rather than code rewrites.

3. **Continuous Learning Integration**: The system improves its recommendations based on successful proposal patterns and user feedback.

4. **Seamless Human-AI Collaboration**: Rather than replacing human expertise, the system amplifies it, providing intelligent assistance while keeping researchers in control of their scientific narrative.

## Measuring Success

How do we know it works? Beyond technical metrics, success will ultimately be measured by the proposals it helps create and fund. Early testing shows significant improvements in several key areas:

- **Time Reduction**: Proposal development time reduced from months to weeks
- **Compliance Accuracy**: 95%+ success rate in meeting format and content requirements
- **Content Quality**: Systematic improvement in NIH rubric scoring across all evaluated sections
- **Literature Integration**: More comprehensive and relevant citation networks

# Part Two: The Related Work Assistant

Anyone who has written an academic paper knows the wall that is the Related Work section. You have the idea, you have the experiments, you have the results, and then you spend days searching databases, reading abstracts for relevance, grouping papers into themes, synthesizing across dozens of studies and formatting citations to a venue's satisfaction. The second system takes a plain-language research description and returns a publication-ready literature review.

The insight is the same one behind the proposal assistant: writing a review is not one task but six distinct ones, and a single model asked to do all six does each of them adequately and none of them well. So there are six agents.

| Agent | Role | Task |
|---|---|---|
| **Input Parser** | Research analyst | Extracts goals, gaps, methodology, keywords and constraints from the description. |
| **Search** | Research librarian | Formulates search strategies and queries OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar, with quality filters and deduplication across sources. |
| **Analysis** | Senior researcher | Summarizes each paper's contribution, identifies methods and findings, scores relevance from 1 to 10 with justification, and assigns themes. |
| **Organization** | Academic editor | Groups papers into topics and subtopics, plans the narrative order, and identifies gaps and controversies. |
| **Writer** | Academic writer | Synthesizes across studies rather than listing them, holding to academic tone and to the length and citation limits. |
| **Reviewer** | Journal reviewer | Assesses comprehensiveness, balance, citation accuracy and clarity, scores the result and names specific improvements. |

## The Loop That Makes It Work

The agents run in sequence, but the sequence is not a pipeline that terminates. The reviewer scores the draft, and if the score falls below the threshold, by default 8.5 out of 10, the system diagnoses which stage is responsible and returns to it: too few papers sends it back to search with expanded queries, poor structure back to organization, weak synthesis back to the writer. It runs up to three iterations before finalizing.

This is the part worth carrying forward. The reviewer does not merely grade the output, it routes the work back to whichever specialist can fix it, which is what makes the ensemble something other than a sequence of prompts.

## Implementation

The models are mixed by cost and difficulty. Local Ollama models handle the mechanical stages, parsing and search strategy. GPT-4 handles the stages that need reasoning: analysis, writing and review. The split cuts API cost by roughly 60% while leaving the hard stages on the stronger model. Orchestration is LangGraph, as in the proposal assistant, with Pydantic for validation and asynchronous queries running the database searches in parallel.

On a typical run the system analyzes 30 to 50 papers in 5 to 15 minutes, scores 8.2 to 9.1 in human evaluation, and adheres to page and citation limits in 98% of cases.

## The Future of Research Support

This project opens the door to a new category of research support tools—AI systems that understand not just language, but the specific challenges and requirements of scientific work. As these systems evolve, they could become indispensable partners in the research process, helping scientists navigate an increasingly complex funding landscape while maintaining focus on discovery and innovation.

The transformation from web development assistant to research proposal expert demonstrates the remarkable adaptability of modern AI systems. More importantly, it shows how thoughtful application of AI technology can address real-world challenges in specialized domains.

We're not just building better tools—we're building a future where brilliant research ideas have the best possible chance of receiving the support they deserve. And in a world facing challenges that will require breakthrough scientific solutions, that's a future worth investing in.

---

*The complete system is open source and available for researchers, institutions, and developers interested in advancing AI-assisted research workflows.*

title: Claus Horn awarded Yale AI for Science Grant
author: EurekaLabs Team
excerpt: An application led by Claus Horn, together with five Yale faculty collaborators, has been awarded the Yale AI for Science grant.
content:
We are delighted to announce that our own Claus Horn has won the Yale AI for Science grant. The application was led by Claus, together with an interdisciplinary team of Yale researchers spanning neurology, immunobiology, genetics, statistics and computer science: **Professor Xianjun Dong** of the Department of Neurology and the Yale Center for RNA Science and Medicine; **Professor Akiko Iwasaki** of the Department of Immunobiology, the Department of Epidemiology of Microbial Diseases and the Department of Dermatology; **Professor Smita Krishnaswamy** of the Department of Genetics and the Department of Computer Science; **Professor Lu Lu** of the Department of Statistics and Data Science; and **Professor Rex Ying** of the Department of Computer Science.

Progress in AI for science depends on combining methodological expertise in machine learning with deep domain knowledge in biology and medicine. This team unites both: experimental and clinical scientists working alongside researchers in statistics, geometric deep learning and biomedical data science. The grant will form the basis for interdisciplinary collaborations for the development of new AI for science applications in biomedicine.

Congratulations to Claus and to the entire team. We look forward to sharing more about the work as it progresses.
